content.text: One consequence of going full width that your bullets don't cover: the **year view** is `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(10.5rem, 1fr))`. At 78rem that's ~6 months per row (6+6); on a 1920px monitor with no cap it becomes ~10 per row, i.e. 10 months then 2.

questions.question: How should the year view lay out once the calendar is full width?

options.label: Cap at 6 columns (Recommended)
options.description: Months grow wider instead of multiplying: 6+6 at any desktop width, still reflowing to 4, 3 or 2 on narrower screens. A year always reads as two even rows, and the extra width goes into readable day cells.

options.label: Fixed 4 columns on desktop
options.description: A classic wall-planner 4×3 at any width ≥600px, reflowing freely below that. Widest, most readable month cells; three rows means the year may need scrolling.

options.label: Leave auto-fill as it is
options.description: No change: months stay ~10.5rem minimum and a wide monitor packs as many per row as fit, so a year can read as 10 months then 2.

All resolved. Here's what I'm writing into the docs:

| | Decision |
|---|---|
| Width | `#cal` loses its 78rem cap; `.view.vK .kb` gets `max-width: 78rem; margin-inline: auto`. Pane always full width |
| Pane | `[board] [zoom]` … `‹ label ›` … `[☰] [⌂]` — still four controls |
| Label | Opens the picker in every view, both platforms. Caret gone. Hover/press states as the affordance. Text unchanged |
| Zoom | New magnifier button in the filter's slot; anchored dropdown; calendar → day/week/month/year, board → vertical/horizontal, current one marked |
| Hamburger | New `menu` icon in the gear's slot; centred panel titled "Calendar": **Filter** section (groups folded; important/assignee on the board) above **Settings** section (nine rows unchanged) |
| Board | Vertical stacks all three stages, pager only in horizontal; drag works in both; orientation stored per device, default horizontal |
| Spacing | `.tb-mid` gap 1rem on desktop only; phone's `‹ ›` take the top row's `clamp(1.3rem, 5.2vw, 1.9rem)` |
| Year view | Capped at 6 columns |

Carried assumptions: the board stays capped in *both* orientations; a vertical board taller than the window scrolls the page vertically (horizontal movement is still forbidden everywhere); zoom level, anchor and sprint still reset on open.

With no `settings.md` at all the anchor is `2024-01-01`, a Monday, and the interval is 2 weeks.
That fallback is a constant rather than anything read off the device, so two devices still agree
on the numbering before the file exists.

They are in the repo because the sprint a task belongs to is *derived* from them. On the device
they would make the same file report a different sprint on a phone than on a laptop, and moving
a card would then write the wrong date. Everything else — theme, date format, time zone, week
start, show-calendar-weeks, the group filter — is a device preference in IndexedDB, the group
filter under `calendar.hiddenGroups` as it already is. Theme and date format are Mine-wide keys,
not the calendar's.

## Sprints

There is no `sprint` key. Sprint *n* runs from `anchor + (n-1) × interval` weeks for `interval`
weeks, and a task's sprint is whichever range its `start` falls in. So:

- the number can never contradict the date, because there is only the date;
- moving a card to another sprint is a write of `start` and `end` and nothing else;
- changing the interval renumbers every card at once, which is correct — it is one timeline.

Computed on bare dates in whole days, never through a `Date` at local midnight: the anchor is a
bare date and sprint boundaries must not shift by a day with the viewer's zone. A `start` before
the anchor has no sprint and the card is not on the board.

## Time zone

One IANA zone name, defaulting to `Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone`, decides
which day a timed entry falls in, its minute offset within that day, and what a wall-clock time
typed into the form means. A bare date never goes near it.

The offset is read off the zone's own wall clock with `Intl.DateTimeFormat.formatToParts`, so
daylight saving comes for free and no table is needed. Converting a typed time to the stored
instant takes **two passes**, because the offset depends on the answer: a time within an hour of
a DST change resolves on the first pass with the wrong offset and on the second with the right
one. A wall-clock time that does not exist — the hour a zone skips in spring — resolves onto the
real time just before the gap, which is stable: it reads back as that time instead of drifting on
every save.

Read the hour with `% 24`: some engines answer `24` for midnight under `hour12: false`.

An unknown zone name falls back to the device's rather than throwing, because a bad value in
settings must not stop the calendar rendering.

## Modules

```
calendar/data.js      the model, the date and sprint arithmetic, and the writes
calendar/ui.js        DOM helpers, the icon set, and the state every view reads
calendar/views.js     year, month, week, day, and the day preview
calendar/kanban.js    the board
calendar/popup.js     the entry popup and its field sub-popups
calendar/settings.js  the settings panel
calendar/app.js       the top pane, navigation, the picker, the filter, the sync line
shared/prefs.js       theme and date format, which belong to Mine rather than to one app
```

`ui.js` holds the state in one object with `render`, `status`, `push` and `reload` as slots the
shell fills in, so a view can ask for a redraw or a background push without importing `app.js`
back and making an import cycle.

`FIELDS` in `popup.js` is built while the module is still evaluating, so anything it calls must
be a function *declaration* — a `const` arrow is still in its temporal dead zone at that point.

**There are two overlay mechanisms and no third.** `openPop` positions a dropdown under the
button that opened it, which only the date picker and the filter do; everything else carries
`.centred` and is only unhidden, by `openCentred`. A third mechanism is how the day preview came
to be anchored by script and then dragged back to the middle with `left: 50% !important` — one
rule undoing another, in two files.

Every icon comes from the one table in `ui.js`. The buttons in `index.html` are empty and are
filled by `icon()` at boot, so an icon cannot drift between a hand-written path in the markup and
the table the views draw from.

## Entry popup

The popup **opens in the middle of the screen**, on a phone as much as on a desktop — and so
does every other overlay in the calendar: a field's own popup, the settings panel and the day
preview. Nothing rises from the bottom edge any more. A centred card is reached with either
thumb and does not pretend to be a drawer that can be dragged.

**An entry that already exists opens read-only.** Clicking an entry — in any grid, in the day
preview, or as a card on the board — opens a **view popup** that shows it, and a pen in that
popup's top row opens the **edit popup**. Most openings are to read: what day is this on, what is
on the agenda, who is coming. A form answers those questions in input boxes, which are harder to
read than text, and it leaves every value one slip away from being changed by a tap meant to
scroll. A new entry has nothing to read, so the `+` and a click on empty space open the edit
popup directly.

### The view popup

A top row, and then the entry. The row carries **the type as a marker, not a choice** — a ticked
square for a task, a calendar page for an event, shown and not pressable — and then,
right-aligned, a trashcan to delete the entry, a **pen** to edit it, and an `x` to close:

```
[☑]                          [trash] [pen] [x]
```

The trashcan stays here rather than moving behind the pen. Deleting is not an edit of a field, and
the board's rule that a card is deleted from its popup in two taps depends on the trashcan being
on the first of them.

Below the row: the title, when it is, and then **only the fields that are set**, in the canonical
order the edit popup's rows use. An entry with a title and a date shows a title and a date.
Nothing here is a row waiting to be filled — that is what the pen is for — so an unset field has
nothing to say and is left out, which also means the set-first ordering below is simply the
canonical order here.

**The details body is shown in full and rendered**, not clipped to two lines and not as raw
markdown, by [Mine's shared renderer](../REQUIREMENTS.md#markdown-bodies). Two lines on a card and
the whole text here are the difference between a glance and having opened the thing.

**A repeating entry says so**, and carries its `skip this one`: skipping drops a single
occurrence, which is an action on the entry like deleting it, not a change to a field. The scope
pair is not here — it governs what an edit writes, and in a popup that writes nothing it would
read as a choice about what you are looking at.

### The edit popup

A row of icon buttons at the top, and it holds the type pair and the three on the right and
nothing between them. **Every button in it is an icon; no button carries a letter.**

- Leftmost, a ticked square for **task** and a calendar page for **event**. Choosing one
  deselects the other; the default is event. What the entry *is* comes first, because it governs
  what the rest of the popup offers. **On an entry that already exists the pair is disabled** —
  it shows which of the two this is and refuses to change it. A task turned into an event drops
  its stage, its importance and its estimate, and a popup opened to fix a typo is not where that
  belongs one tap away. The type is settled when the entry is made.
- Then, right-aligned: a trashcan to delete the entry, a disk to save it, and an `x` to close and
  discard. **The `x` is rightmost, in every popup in Mine.** The way out of an overlay sits in the
  same corner wherever you are, so leaving one is never something to look for — and that corner
  is worth more to the button you reach for by habit than to the one you aim at. The disk gives
  it up and sits beside it.

There is no dash between the two groups: the gap to the right-aligned trio already separates
them, and the field icons the dash used to divide off are not in this row at all any more.

Below it, in this order: the **title**, the **start and end** fields, the **toggle row**, and
then **one row per field**.

### The toggle row

One row of icons directly under start and end. These are not fields with a form each: they are
small values, edited in the row itself, and they **show their value** rather than merely whether
they have one — each as a small badge on the corner of its icon.

- **`24h` for all-day** — the one control in the popup that is a word rather than a picture, and
  deliberately so: every drawing of a whole day reads as something else. The sun it replaces was
  taken for weather or for daylight hours, and `24h` cannot be. **A clickable control, not a
  checkbox** — lit when on, plain when off. On an event it is alone on the row. Only the button
  changes its name: the strip in the week and day grids still reads `all-day`, and so does this
  document, because the word is the clearer one in prose and the button is the one place with no
  room for it.
- three small columns for **stage** — cycles `todo` → `doing` → `done` on each tap, its badge in
  that stage's kanban colour: red, yellow, green. There is no stage popup.
- a `!` for **important** — a straight toggle, lit when the task is important and plain when it
  is not. It carries no badge: a yes or no has nothing a badge could add that the lit state has
  not already said, which is what made the old flag need a digit and this one not.
- an hourglass for **estimate** — the one that opens a popup, because a number has to be typed.
  Its badge reads the day count as `2d`. It stays on this row rather than joining the field rows
  below, because what it carries is a badge-sized value like the other three, not a form.

On an event, stage, important and estimate are not there at all, because an event has none of
them. They sit here so that a task that is not on a board still carries the two fields a kanban
card edits.

Neither lit control — `24h` or `!` — is the save button's green: in all of Mine green is a save
and red is a trashcan, and a green toggle beside the disk would make the popup look like it
offers two primary actions.

### The field rows

Every other field is a row, and **every field has a row, set or not** — the rows are now the only
way to reach a field, so none of them can be hidden. A row is the icon on the left and the
field's name beside it, and, when the field is set, its value after that:

```
[ball]    Category     Work
[pin]     Location     Conference room 3B
[lines]   Details
[repeat]  Repeat
```

The six fields, in their canonical order:

- three lines of text for **details** — the markdown body;
- a ball for **category**;
- circular arrows for **repetition**;
- a bell for **alerts**;
- a pin for **location**;
- a person for **participants**.

- **Clicking a row opens that field's popup.** The row *is* the pen, so no row carries one, and

- **The rows that are set move to the top.** Set fields come first, unset ones follow, and inside
  each group the order is always the canonical one above. Setting a field lifts its row into the
  top group and shuffles nothing else, so a row never moves for a reason you did not cause.
- **A set row is plain.** Being in the top group and showing a value is what says the field is
  set — which is what the old lit icon said, in a row that no longer exists. Nothing in the
  popup lights except the two toggles on the row above, `24h` and `!`.

Each of the six opens its own popup, and every popup has the same three buttons in the entry
popup's own order: a trashcan that clears that one field, a disk that commits the value into the
entry form, and, rightmost, an `x` that abandons the sub-edit. **A sub-popup never writes to the

content.text: The merge is the big one — it's load-bearing for several documented rules. Let me check how the write queue behaves first, because it decides whether per-field saving is viable.

Queue mechanics: each save calls `enqueue({op:'put', path, text, baseOid})` and `S.push()`, and drains are serialised — so **one field save becomes one commit**. Today an entry edit is one commit no matter how many fields changed, which `calendar/REQUIREMENTS.md` states explicitly ("Nothing is written until the entry popup's own disk, so one entry edit is one commit").

## Entry popup

The popup **opens in the middle of the screen**, on a phone as much as on a desktop — and so
does every other overlay in the calendar: a field's own popup, the settings panel and the day
preview. Nothing rises from the bottom edge any more. A centred card is reached with either
thumb and does not pretend to be a drawer that can be dragged.

**An entry that already exists opens read-only.** Clicking an entry — in any grid, in the day
preview, or as a card on the board — opens a **view popup** that shows it, and a pen in that
popup's top row opens the **edit popup**. Most openings are to read: what day is this on, what is
on the agenda, who is coming. A form answers those questions in input boxes, which are harder to
read than text, and it leaves every value one slip away from being changed by a tap meant to
scroll. A new entry has nothing to read, so the `+` and a click on empty space open the edit
popup directly.

### The view popup

## Entry popup

The popup **opens in the middle of the screen**, on a phone as much as on a desktop — and so
does every other overlay in the calendar: the hamburger panel and the day preview. Nothing rises
from the bottom edge any more. A centred card is reached with either thumb and does not pretend
to be a drawer that can be dragged.

**There is one popup, and it is both.** Clicking an entry — in any grid, in the day preview, or
as a card on the board — opens the entry, shown as text, and **every value in it is edited where
it is read**: click the thing, change it, save it. There is no pen, no second popup behind one,
and no mode to be in.

It was two before, a read-only preview with a pen into a form, and the reason was sound: a form
answers *what day is this on* in input boxes, which are harder to read than text and leave every
value one slip away from a tap meant to scroll. Editing in place keeps that — a row is text until
it is clicked, so there is still nothing to slip into — and gives back the two things the split
cost. A change was four taps: open, pen, field, save. And the preview and the form had to agree
about every field twice over, in two blocks of code, which is how one of them came to show the
stage and the other to hide it.

**Each row saves itself, and a save reaches the repo.** There is no disk in the top row, because
there is no draft to commit: the row's own save writes the file and queues the push, and the sync
line reports it as it reports every other write. One entry edited in four fields is therefore up
to four commits where it used to be one — the price of the popup always showing what is actually
stored, and a fair one against a history whose job is to be readable.

```
[☑]                                  [trash] [x]      an entry that exists
[☑] [📅]                                       [x]    a new one: the type is still a choice
```

The top row carries **the type**, then right-aligned a trashcan to delete the entry and an `x` to
close. On an entry that already exists the type is a **marker, not a choice** — a ticked square
for a task, a calendar page for an event, shown and not pressable — because a task turned into an
event drops its stage, its importance and its estimate, and the type is settled when the entry is
made. On a new entry it is the pair, with the event selected.

The trashcan stays at the left of that group rather than beside the `x`: deleting is not an edit
of a field, and the board's rule that a card is deleted from its popup in two taps depends on the
trashcan being on the first of them.

Below the row, in this order: the **title**, the **scope and skip** row on a repeating entry, the
**when**, the **toggle row**, **one row per field**, and the **details body** last.

### A row, and a row being edited

Every row is **the icon, then the value** — no field name beside it:

```
[ball]    Work                                      [trash]
[pin]     Conference room 3B                        [trash]
[repeat]  Repeat
[bell]    Alerts
```

The name is gone because it said the same thing as the icon it sat beside, in the one column
where the value has to fit. **An unset row shows the field's name in its place, muted** — which
is what an empty input does everywhere else in Mine, and what keeps a bell from being a bell and
nothing else. A set row reads as a value; an unset one reads as an invitation.

- **The rows that are set move to the top.** Set fields come first, unset ones follow, and inside
  each group the order is always the canonical one below. Setting a field lifts its row into the
  top group and shuffles nothing else, so a row never moves for a reason you did not cause.
- **A set row carries a trashcan at its right**, which clears that field and writes at once. An
  unset row has nothing to clear and carries none. There is no prompt: a cleared field is typed
  again, which is not what a deleted entry is.
- **Clicking a row makes it active.** The value becomes the control for it, in the row itself, and
  the row's right-hand end becomes **trashcan, save, `x`** — the same three in the same order as
  every popup in Mine, which is where that field's own popup used to put them. The save writes;
  the `x` abandons what was typed; the trashcan clears the field.
- **Only one row is active at a time.** Clicking another row while one is active is the same as
  that row's `x`, and asks the same question if there is something to lose.
- **Clicking a row's trashcan does not activate the row.** This is the rule a kanban card already
  holds to, and it matters more here, because the trashcan now sits on the surface being tapped.
  The row and its controls are one place where a click that does two things is easy to build.

The six fields, in their canonical order:

- three lines of text for **details** — the markdown body;
- a ball for **category**;
- circular arrows for **repetition**;
- a bell for **alerts**;
- a pin for **location**;
- a person for **participants**.

**Every editor opens in its own row.** There is no popup over the popup any more: the field
popups are gone, and with them the rule that a sub-popup never writes to the repo, which has
nothing left to govern. The card scrolls, so a textarea fits in a row as well as it fitted in a
card of its own. The one survivor of that mechanism is the group manager behind *edit groups*,
which is not editing a field.

**Picking a category saves it.** Tapping a group writes it into the entry and closes the row —
there is nothing more to say about a choice from a list, and a save would only confirm what the
tap already said. Its active row therefore carries a trashcan and an `x` and **no save**, the one
row in the popup that does. Everywhere else a value is typed or combined, and the save stays.

### The title, the when, and the toggle row

**The title is a row too** — text until clicked, then an input with the trio. So is **the when**,
which reads `MON, 20.11.2026 · 09:00–10:00` and opens the start and end date and time inputs
inside the row. Four input boxes at the top of a popup opened to find out what day something is
on was the form at its least readable, and this is the row that had the most to gain.

The when-line no longer repeats the stage, the importance and the estimate as words. The toggle
row shows all three, live, directly beneath it.

### The toggle row

One row of icons directly under the when. These are not fields with an editor each: they are
small values, edited in the row itself with a single tap, and they **show their value** rather
than merely whether they have one — each as a small badge on the corner of its icon.

**A tap on one of them writes.** They are the one part of the popup with no save, because a tap
*is* the whole edit — which is already what a board card's `<` `>` do, so it is not a new rule
and not a new way to lose a change.

- **`24h` for all-day** — the one control in the popup that is a word rather than a picture, and
  deliberately so: every drawing of a whole day reads as something else. The sun it replaces was
  taken for weather or for daylight hours, and `24h` cannot be. **A clickable control, not a
  checkbox** — lit when on, plain when off. On an event it is alone on the row. Only the button
  changes its name: the strip in the week and day grids still reads `all-day`, and so does this
  document, because the word is the clearer one in prose and the button is the one place with no
  room for it.
- three small columns for **stage** — cycles `todo` → `doing` → `done` on each tap, its badge in
  that stage's kanban colour: red, yellow, green. There is no stage popup.
- a `!` for **important** — a straight toggle, lit when the task is important and plain when it
  is not. It carries no badge: a yes or no has nothing a badge could add that the lit state has
  not already said, which is what made the old flag need a digit and this one not.
- an hourglass for **estimate** — the one of the four that opens an editor, because a number has
  to be typed. It opens **inline, beneath the row**, with the trio, like any other field. Its
  badge reads the day count as `2d`.

On an event, stage, important and estimate are not there at all, because an event has none of
them. They sit here so that a task that is not on a board still carries the two fields a kanban
card edits.

Neither lit control — `24h` or `!` — is a save's green: in all of Mine green is a save and red is
a trashcan, and a green toggle would make a lit flag read as a commit.

### The details body

Last in the popup, and **shown in full and rendered** — not clipped to two lines, not as raw
markdown — by [Mine's shared renderer](../REQUIREMENTS.md#markdown-bodies). Two lines on a card
and the whole text here are the difference between a glance and having opened the thing, and that
is the one thing the old preview existed for, so it is not spent on making the body look like the
rows above it.

It carries a small header of its own: the `lines` icon, and the trashcan at the right when there
is a body to clear. **Clicking the body makes it active**, replacing the rendered text with the
raw markdown in a textarea and putting the trio at its foot. A body is read far more often than
it is written, which is the same argument the rows make, with more text behind it.

### A new entry

A new entry has nothing to read and no file to write to, so it opens **with its title row already
active** and the when seeded from wherever it was made — the cell, the day preview's `+`, or a
kanban column header, which seeds the stage as well.

**Saving the title creates the entry.** Until then there is nothing to write a field into, so the
other rows are inert and drawn dimmed, and closing the popup writes nothing at all — a `+` opened
and thought better of leaves no file and no commit. Once the title is saved the entry exists and
every row behaves as it does on any other entry.

That is why the title is the row that creates it: an entry must have one, so it is the only field
whose first save can be the file's first save.

### A repeating entry

A repeating entry says so under the title, and carries two things the rest do not:

- **the scope pair**, `this occurrence` or `whole series`, which governs **every row saved while
  the popup is open**. It has to be visible and it has to be one choice: asked again at each
  save it would be a prompt on every field, and left implicit it would be the kind of thing that
  silently rewrites a rule. It is set before the row it applies to, which is the order the two
  controls already sit in.
- **`skip this one`**, which drops a single occurrence. That is an action on the entry like
  deleting it, not a change to a field, so it sits with the scope rather than among the rows.

Only the series carries the rule, so **the repetition row is absent on an occurrence override** —
a rule the popup must not rewrite has no row at all.

### Saving, and leaving

A row's save **writes the file, closes the row back to text, and leaves the popup open**. The
push runs in the background and is reported in the sync line, not in the row: you stay where you
were, looking at the entry you just changed, which is the whole point of editing in place.

Deleting the entry and skipping an occurrence both close the popup and land on the calendar,
because neither leaves anything to look at.

### Discarding an edit

**The only unsaved work in the popup is what is typed in the active row**, so that is what the
prompt guards. Pressing the row's `x`, pressing the popup's `x`, clicking the backdrop or pressing
Escape, while an active row has been modified, are one way out and ask one question: a small
centred prompt offering **discard** or **keep editing**. An untouched row closes without a word —
the question is about losing work, and there is none to lose. A half-written new entry counts as
work, which here is the same statement: its title row is the row that has been typed into.

The prompt carries a **don't ask again** toggle. Ticking it silences the prompt on that device for
good, so the `x` goes straight back to discarding. That is a preference about this screen's
behaviour rather than data, so it is stored on the device like the rest of them — and it has a
row in the panel's settings section, because nothing in Mine may be switched off from a place
that cannot switch it back on.

**A saved row is not something a discard can reach.** It is in the file. This is the one thing the
merge genuinely changes about losing work: there is far less of it to lose at any moment, and
what has been saved is gone from the prompt's reach for good.

b="""## Writes from the popup

One row's save is one write. The title's first save on a new entry is `createEntry`; every save
after that is `updateEntry`, or `saveOverride` when the scope pair says `this occurrence`. The
popup stays open, so this is the first place in the app that writes the same entry repeatedly
from one screen, and three things follow that the save-once-and-close popup never had to handle.

**The popup re-points at the saved entry after every write.** `S.reload()` rebuilds the model, so
the occurrence object the popup was opened with is stale the moment a row saves: its `data` is a
generation behind and its `baseOid` with it. The popup must take the reloaded occurrence and draw
from that. Holding the old object is the bug this note exists for, and it does not look like one
— the row shows the right value, because the row put it there, and only the *next* row's save
goes out with a stale base and lands as a conflict against a file the user themselves just wrote.

**A date change moves the file.** The day is in the path and the API has no rename, so the when
row's save is a delete plus a create — and the popup must then follow the entry to its new path,
for the same reason. A popup still pointing at the old path writes a file that no longer exists.

**A drain collapses queued writes per path.** Several saves can queue before a drain — offline,
or faster than the chain runs — and `POST /git/trees` is handed one entry per queued item, so the
same path would appear more than once in a single tree. The drain keeps the **last** text for a
path and drops the earlier entries. The `baseOid` needs no choosing: `putFile` leaves the local
`oid` alone on a queued write, so every queued put for a path already carries the same base, which
is the one the first edit was made against and the right one to detect a real conflict with.

**Nothing writes before the entry exists.** On a new entry the rows other than the title are
inert — not merely ignored on click, but drawn as such — because there is no file to patch and no
path to patch it at. The title's save is what creates both.

## Modules
"""
assert a in s; s=s.replace(a,b,1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("ok")

## Entry popup

The popup **opens in the middle of the screen**, on a phone as much as on a desktop — and so
does every other overlay in the calendar: the hamburger panel and the day preview. Nothing rises
from the bottom edge any more. A centred card is reached with either thumb and does not pretend
to be a drawer that can be dragged.

**There is one popup, and it is both.** Clicking an entry — in any grid, in the day preview, or
as a card on the board — opens the entry, shown as text, and **every value in it is edited where
it is read**: click the thing, change it, save it. There is no pen, no second popup behind one,
and no mode to be in.

It was two before, a read-only preview with a pen into a form, and the reason was sound: a form
answers *what day is this on* in input boxes, which are harder to read than text and leave every
value one slip away from a tap meant to scroll. Editing in place keeps that — a row is text until
it is clicked, so there is still nothing to slip into — and gives back the two things the split
cost. A change was four taps: open, pen, field, save. And the preview and the form had to agree
about every field twice over, in two blocks of code, which is how one of them came to show the
stage and the other to hide it.

**Each row saves itself, and a save reaches the repo.** There is no disk in the top row, because
there is no draft to commit: the row's own save writes the file and queues the push, and the sync
line reports it as it reports every other write. One entry edited in four fields is therefore up
to four commits where it used to be one — the price of the popup always showing what is actually
stored, and a fair one against a history whose job is to be readable.

```
[☑]                                  [trash] [x]      an entry that exists
[☑] [📅]                                       [x]    a new one: the type is still a choice
```

The top row carries **the type**, then right-aligned a trashcan to delete the entry and an `x` to
close. On an entry that already exists the type is a **marker, not a choice** — a ticked square
for a task, a calendar page for an event, shown and not pressable — because a task turned into an
event drops its stage, its importance and its estimate, and the type is settled when the entry is
made. On a new entry it is the pair, with the event selected.

The trashcan stays at the left of that group rather than beside the `x`: deleting is not an edit
of a field, and the board's rule that a card is deleted from its popup in two taps depends on the
trashcan being on the first of them.

Below the row, in this order: the **title**, the **scope and skip** row on a repeating entry, the
**when**, the **toggle row**, **one row per field**, and the **details body** last.

Neither lit control — `24h` or `!` — is a save's green: in all of Mine green is a save and red is
a trashcan, and a green toggle would make a lit flag read as a commit.

### The details body

Last in the popup, and **shown in full and rendered** — not clipped to two lines, not as raw
markdown — by [Mine's shared renderer](../REQUIREMENTS.md#markdown-bodies). Two lines on a card
and the whole text here are the difference between a glance and having opened the thing, and that
is the one thing the old preview existed for, so it is not spent on making the body look like the
rows above it.

It carries a small header of its own: the `lines` icon, and the trashcan at the right when there
is a body to clear. **Clicking the body makes it active**, replacing the rendered text with the
raw markdown in a textarea and putting the trio at its foot. A body is read far more often than
it is written, which is the same argument the rows make, with more text behind it.

### A new entry

A new entry has nothing to read and no file to write to, so it opens **with its title row already
active** and the when seeded from wherever it was made — the cell, the day preview's `+`, or a
kanban column header, which seeds the stage as well.

**Saving the title creates the entry.** Until then there is nothing to write a field into, so the
other rows are inert and drawn dimmed, and closing the popup writes nothing at all — a `+` opened
and thought better of leaves no file and no commit. Once the title is saved the entry exists and
every row behaves as it does on any other entry.

That is why the title is the row that creates it: an entry must have one, so it is the only field
whose first save can be the file's first save.

### A repeating entry

A repeating entry says so under the title, and carries two things the rest do not:

- **the scope pair**, `this occurrence` or `whole series`, which governs **every row saved while
  the popup is open**. It has to be visible and it has to be one choice: asked again at each
  save it would be a prompt on every field, and left implicit it would be the kind of thing that
  silently rewrites a rule. It is set before the row it applies to, which is the order the two
  controls already sit in.
- **`skip this one`**, which drops a single occurrence. That is an action on the entry like
  deleting it, not a change to a field, so it sits with the scope rather than among the rows.

Only the series carries the rule, so **the repetition row is absent on an occurrence override** —
a rule the popup must not rewrite has no row at all.

### Saving, and leaving

A row's save **writes the file, closes the row back to text, and leaves the popup open**. The
push runs in the background and is reported in the sync line, not in the row: you stay where you
were, looking at the entry you just changed, which is the whole point of editing in place.

Deleting the entry and skipping an occurrence both close the popup and land on the calendar,
because neither leaves anything to look at.

### Discarding an edit

**The only unsaved work in the popup is what is typed in the active row**, so that is what the
prompt guards. Pressing the row's `x`, pressing the popup's `x`, clicking the backdrop or pressing
Escape, while an active row has been modified, are one way out and ask one question: a small
centred prompt offering **discard** or **keep editing**. An untouched row closes without a word —
the question is about losing work, and there is none to lose. A half-written new entry counts as
work, which here is the same statement: its title row is the row that has been typed into.

The prompt carries a **don't ask again** toggle. Ticking it silences the prompt on that device for
good, so the `x` goes straight back to discarding. That is a preference about this screen's
behaviour rather than data, so it is stored on the device like the rest of them — and it has a
row in the panel's settings section, because nothing in Mine may be switched off from a place
that cannot switch it back on.

content.text:
Done. Summary of what the merge changed in the docs:

**`calendar/REQUIREMENTS.md`** — `## Entry popup` and its subsections rewritten:

| | Decision recorded |
|---|---|
| Structure | One popup. Top row = type (marker when it exists, live pair when new), trashcan, `x`. **No pen, no disk** |
| Rows | `icon + value`; unset shows the field's name muted; set rows sort to top |
| Editing | Click a row → editor **inside the row**, right end becomes the canonical **trashcan, save, `x`**; one active row at a time; a row's trashcan doesn't activate the row |
| Saves | A row's save **writes the file and queues the push** — up to four commits for a four-field edit, stated as the accepted price |
| Fields | **Five** rows (category, repeat, alerts, location, participants); **details is the body**, rendered in full at the foot under an icon+trashcan header, clicked to become a textarea |
| Category | A tap on a group **is** the save; its active row has trashcan and `x`, **no save**. Repetition explicitly does *not* commit on dropdown change |
| Title / when | Both are click-to-activate rows; the when reads `MON, 20.11.2026 · 09:00–10:00` and opens the four inputs inline |
| Toggles | Stay one-tap and write through — justified against the board card's `<` `>`, which already does |
| New entry | Title row active on open, other rows inert and dimmed; **saving the title creates the file**; abandoning a `+` writes nothing |
| Repeating | Scope pair + `skip this one` under the title, governing every row saved while open — which reverses the old "the scope pair is not here" rule, and says why |
| Discard | Narrowed to the active row; a saved row is past the prompt's reach; `Confirm discard` row stays, so the panel stays at nine |

**`calendar/TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md`** — new `## Writes from the popup` section with the three hazards write-through introduces, plus the module list and the overlay rule (`#sub` now exists only for the group manager; one builder, no `viewCard` beside `fillForm`).

**`TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md`** — the read-only/pen/sub-popup checks replaced with checks for the merged popup, including the ones that must now come out the *opposite* way (the scope pair is present; no pen anywhere) so a copied old assertion can't survive.

Three things I'd flag for implementation:

1. **The stale-occurrence bug is the real risk here.** The popup holds the occurrence it was opened with; after the first row's save that object is a generation behind, and the *second* save goes out against a dead base — landing as a conflict against a file the user just wrote, while the first row still displays correctly. It's documented in both the technical and test docs because it will not look like a bug.
2. **A date save moves the file** (the day is in the path, no rename API), so the popup has to follow the entry to its new path or the next save writes a file that no longer exists.
3. **Queued writes to one path now collide.** Several saves can queue before a drain, and `POST /git/trees` would get the same path more than once. The documented fix is to collapse per path keeping the last text — the `baseOid` needs no choosing, since `putFile` leaves the local `oid` alone on a queued write.
can we fix the flags by making row changes not a direct save but only when task/event is saved when closing? e.g. save button appears if row changes. Would be fine for me as well

Yes — and it's the better trade. Going back to a draft kills all three hazards at once: no stale occurrence (one write, at the end), no mid-edit path move, no queued writes colliding on one path. It also restores "one entry edit is one commit", which the write-through model was spending.

What it costs is the thing write-through bought: the popup no longer always shows what's stored. A row saved and left looks committed when it isn't — which is exactly why "the save button appears only when something changed" matters, so let me pin down what that button is.

### A new entry

A new entry has nothing to read and no file to write to, so it opens **with its title row already
active** and the when seeded from wherever it was made — the cell, the day preview's `+`, or a
kanban column header, which seeds the stage as well.

**Saving the title creates the entry.** Until then there is nothing to write a field into, so the
other rows are inert and drawn dimmed, and closing the popup writes nothing at all — a `+` opened
and thought better of leaves no file and no commit. Once the title is saved the entry exists and
every row behaves as it does on any other entry.

That is why the title is the row that creates it: an entry must have one, so it is the only field
whose first save can be the file's first save.

### A repeating entry

A repeating entry says so under the title, and carries two things the rest do not:

- **the scope pair**, `this occurrence` or `whole series`, which governs **every row saved while
  the popup is open**. It has to be visible and it has to be one choice: asked again at each
  save it would be a prompt on every field, and left implicit it would be the kind of thing that
  silently rewrites a rule. It is set before the row it applies to, which is the order the two
  controls already sit in.
- **`skip this one`**, which drops a single occurrence. That is an action on the entry like
  deleting it, not a change to a field, so it sits with the scope rather than among the rows.

Only the series carries the rule, so **the repetition row is absent on an occurrence override** —
a rule the popup must not rewrite has no row at all.

new = """## Writes from the popup

The popup holds a draft and writes once. The disk is `createEntry` on a new entry, `updateEntry`
on a saved one, and `saveOverride` when the scope pair says `this occurrence` — so **one entry
edit is one commit**, and the occurrence the popup was opened with stays valid for as long as the
popup is open, because nothing has moved under it.

**Per-row write-through was considered and rejected**, and the reasons are worth keeping, because
each of them is invisible until it bites:

- the popup would have to re-point at the saved entry after every write. `S.reload()` rebuilds
  the model, so the occurrence held by the popup is a generation stale the moment a row saves,
  and its `baseOid` with it. The row that saved looks perfectly correct — it put the value there
  itself — and the *next* row's save goes out against a dead base and lands as a conflict against
  a file the user just wrote;
- a date change moves the file, the day being in the path and the API having no rename, so the
  popup would have to follow the entry to a new path mid-edit or write to one that no longer
  exists;
- several saves can queue before a drain, offline or faster than the chain runs, and
  `POST /git/trees` is handed one entry per queued item — so the same path would appear more than
  once in one tree, which the save-once popup cannot produce.

A draft has none of these, and the only thing it gives up is that the popup shows a value the
file does not yet hold. The disk appearing exactly when the two differ is what says so.

**`snapshot(D)` is what the disk and the prompt both read.** It already exists for the discard
prompt: the draft's editable parts, serialised, compared against the baseline taken when the
popup opened. The disk's presence is the same comparison, so there is one definition of *changed*

touched has **no disk**; that changing any one thing — a row, a toggle, the title, the when —
makes one appear; and that putting it back by hand makes it **go away again**, which is the check

touch. That the disk is the **only** control in the popup that writes: no row, no toggle and no

the two-saves confusion this rule exists against. That the row's `x` **puts that row back as it
was** and leaves the rest of the draft alone: typed into two rows, reverting one keeps the other.

write-through design could not make, and it is the reason for the draft, so it is checked as a
count and not as an outcome.

the field in the draft — the row drops to its muted name and the disk appears — and that it does
**not** write on its own. That **clicking a row's trashcan does not activate the row**: the field
is cleared and no input appears, which is the same rule a kanban card holds to and matters more
here, the trashcan now being on the surface being tapped.

**A row shows its value, not its name.** That a set row's text is the value — `Work`, not
`Category Work` — and that the field's name appears **nowhere** in a set row. That an unset row
shows the field's name in its place, in the muted colour and not the plain one, resolved from the
computed colour against the two tokens rather than from a screenshot. That the **five** rows read
category, repeat, alerts, location, participants in that canonical order on a task and on an
event alike, with **details not among them** — it is the body at the foot, and a details row
appearing in the list is the body having been flattened into one; that **every one of the five
has a row whether it is set or not**; and that setting one moves its row above the unset ones
while the order inside each group stays canonical.

it in one tap, with nothing pressed after it, and that **nothing is written** — the queue is
still empty and the disk is now showing. That the repetition row, by contrast, stays open when

and **every other row live** — clicking one opens its editor — with the when seeded from where it

row is inactive — the whole text, not a clipped line — and that clicking it replaces the rendered

content.text:
Switched to the draft model across all three docs.

**What changed from the write-through version:**

| | Now |
|---|---|
| Saves | **One**, in the top row, and it appears only once something differs from the file. It's the only control that writes |
| A row | Trashcan + `x`, **no save**. The `x` puts that one row back; clicking another row or the disk takes what's in it |
| Toggles | Tap changes the draft, not the repo — the disk appears on the first tap |
| Category | A tap on a group still closes the row in one tap; it just stages instead of writing |
| New entry | A draft like any other edit: every row live, when seeded, **disk disabled until the title has text**. The title-first/inert-rows rule is gone |
| Closing | The popup's `x`, backdrop and Escape prompt discard / keep editing, as today; `Confirm discard` stays, panel stays at nine rows. A row's own `x` never prompts |
| Commits | One entry edit is one commit again |

**`calendar/TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md`** — `## Writes from the popup` rewritten: the draft model, then the three write-through faults kept on record as *considered and rejected*, so the idea doesn't come back without them. Plus two new technical requirements the appearing disk creates:

- **`snapshot(D)` drives both the disk and the prompt.** The function already exists for the discard prompt; the disk's visibility must be the same comparison, or a disk that shows when the prompt stays silent (or the reverse) is that one definition having grown a second copy.
- **Switching the scope pair must retake the baseline.** It rebuilds the draft from the other file, and a stale baseline reads as "changed" — which puts a disk in the top row of a popup nobody edited and makes every exit ask about changes nobody made. This was already a latent bug in the old code; the appearing disk makes it visible.

**`TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md`** — the popup checks now include the ones this model needs and the old one couldn't express:

- The disk appears on a change and **goes away again** when it's undone by hand — that's what catches a flag set on first touch rather than a real comparison.
- **One edit is one commit**, checked as a queue count: four things changed, one write.
- Nothing writes before the disk: the queue stays empty through row saves, toggle taps and a category pick.
- A row's `x` reverts only that row and leaves the rest of the draft alone.
- The prompt and the disk agree in both directions.

One thing worth knowing: the "appearing disk" means the top row's control count changes while the popup is open. The `x`-is-rightmost check reads button positions, so it needs to assert the order both with and without the disk present — otherwise a layout that inserts the disk to the right of the `x` passes whenever nothing has been edited yet.
Great work. Now commit the changes. Then implement the features, commit and push. I will then test on my phone/laptop and provide feedback.
